common_name: Crispy Wave Fern (Ruffled Bird's Nest Fern)

planting.note: Plant in loose, well-drained, humus-rich soil in bright indirect shade; Crispy Wave is grown outdoors only in frost-free zones and is otherwise a container or houseplant brought outside for the warm season.

directions: Plant in loose, well-drained, humus-rich soil in bright indirect shade, and keep humidity high — misting or a nearby pebble tray helps outside of naturally humid climates. Crispy Wave is a distinctive bird's nest fern cultivar with broad, undivided, glossy fronds that ripple and ruffle along their edges instead of lying flat like the species, giving each frond a wavy, sculptural texture that stands out among shade foliage plants. Its bold, simple leaf form (unlike the finely divided fronds of most ferns) makes it a striking accent for shaded patios, covered porches, and container groupings in frost-free gardens, and a popular houseplant everywhere else. Avoid overwatering, since the central crown rots readily if water sits in it; water at the soil line rather than into the center of the rosette.

planting.note: Plant in fall or early spring in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in partial to full shade; Jacob is among the earliest-blooming Christmas rose selections, often flowering in early winter.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, slightly alkaline, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil evenly moist through establishment. Jacob is prized as one of the earliest Christmas rose selections to flower, often opening its large, rounded, pure white blooms with a faint pink blush by early winter — well ahead of the traditional Helleborus niger bloom time — giving gardeners a jump on winter color while most other perennials are dormant. The dark, leathery, evergreen foliage stays attractive year-round, providing structure between bloom seasons in a shaded border or woodland garden. Remove old, tattered leaves in late winter just before flowering to best display the blooms, and note that all parts of the plant are toxic if ingested.

planting.note: Plant in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; excellent drainage is essential to prevent crown rot.

Lime Zinger produces bright chartreuse-green succulent foliage edged in a fine, contrasting cherry-red margin, a color combination that intensifies with more sun exposure, topped by clusters of pink summer flowers that draw bees and butterflies. Its compact, mounding habit and season-long foliage color make it a strong choice for rock gardens, border edges, and mixed succulent containers where a low-maintenance, drought-tolerant color accent is wanted. Shear back lightly after flowering to keep the mound dense and tidy, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years to renew vigor.

Dazzleberry pairs cool, powdery blue-green succulent foliage with dense, flat-topped clusters of vivid magenta-pink flowers in late summer, a striking color combination that holds up well through heat and draws bees and butterflies heavily while in bloom. Its sturdy, compact habit resists flopping better than some older sedum cultivars, staying tidy through the growing season without staking. Leave the spent flower heads standing into fall and winter for continued textural interest, and divide congested clumps in spring every few years to renew vigor.

Blue Spruce is a low, trailing sedum with fine, needle-like, powdery blue foliage that closely mimics a miniature conifer, spreading into a dense, textural mat topped with clusters of star-shaped yellow flowers in summer. Its low, spreading habit and cool blue color make it an effective groundcover for rock gardens, gravel gardens, and the edges of raised beds, spilling attractively over rock walls or container edges. It spreads readily but is easy to control by simply pulling or trimming back trailing stems; divide congested patches in spring to renew vigor or propagate new plantings.
